notes:
I've organised these notes verse by verse. Some verses have very little material, and a few have none, because I ran out of searches and page reads before I could cover the whole passage. Two pages I opened (Enduring Word and Precept Austin) were cut off partway through. The gaps are listed at the end.

**v. 1**
- Guzik says each word matters. "Jesus" is a real person in history, "Christ" means Messiah, and "Son of God" means He is the unique Son, who is also God the Son. First, this is the good news of Jesus, a genuine, historical person who walked this earth like other men. It is the good news of the Christ (which simply means "Messiah"), the promised, anointed Savior of men. And it is the good news of the Son of God, and a Son in more than a sense that we think of all men coming from God. Jesus is the unique Son of God, who is also God the Son. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- Guzik cites Lane on "gospel." Romans used the word for announcements about the emperor, and an inscription from about 9 B.C. praising Augustus reads much like Mark's first line. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- Precept Austin points out that Mark calls this the beginning of the message of good news, not just the beginning of his book. Notice that Mark says this is not the beginning of his book, but the beginning of the message of good news. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-1-commentary
- Ryle (quoted on Precept Austin) reads "Son of God" as a claim that Jesus is divine. They were nothing less than an assertion of our Lord's divinity. They were a declaration that Jesus was Himself very God, and "equal with God." https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-1-commentary
- Calvin says Mark shows that redemption can come only from the Son of God. But Mark shows us, that no redemption is to be expected but from *the Son of God* https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/1-1.html
- Gill compares Mark's opening with Paul's first preaching in Acts 9:20. Both begin with Christ's sonship to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/1-1.htm
- The NET Bible note (quoted on Precept Austin) is unsure whether "beginning" covers the whole Gospel, only John's ministry, or echoes Genesis 1:1. It thinks the Genesis echo is most likely, with God starting a "new beginning." https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-1-commentary
- **The words "Son of God" are missing from some manuscripts.**
  - TGC (Mark Strauss): The phrase "Son of God" is textually debated, since some of our earliest manuscripts do not contain this phrase. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/mark/
  - A. T. Robertson: Aleph 28, 255 omit these words, but B, D, L, have them and the great mass of the manuscripts have υιου του θεου. If this is a heading added to what Mark wrote, the heading may have existed early in two forms, one with, one without "Son of God." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rwp/mark-1.html
  - The commentary quoted on StudyLight says the phrase is probably legitimate. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/1-1.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary says the phrase has preponderating manuscript authority. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/mark/1.htm
  - Utley (bible.org) disagrees. He thinks the words look like a deliberate addition by early scribes guarding against the heresy that Jesus only *became* God's Son. https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-1

**vv. 2–3**
- Guzik: Mark's first point about John is that the Old Testament foretold him (Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3). He also calls John the first true prophet to Israel in about 300 years. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- Guzik: John prepared the way for *Jesus*, and the prophecy calls that way the way of "the Lord." So in Mark's mind, Jesus is Lord. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- Guzik: Isaiah's picture is of building a highway for a king, filling the holes and levelling the hills. The real road-building happens in our hearts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- Different manuscripts give "in Isaiah the prophet" or "in the prophets," which is why the BSB and NKJV read differently. The ESV footnote says Some manuscripts *in the prophets*. https://www.blueletterbible.org/esv/mar/1/1/

**v. 4**
- Guzik: Baptism means to immerse. For a Jew, being baptized like a Gentile convert was to admit being as far from God as a Gentile. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- John Phillips (quoted on Precept Austin) says John's baptism could not wash sin away. His baptism could not wash away sin, but his preaching could produce conviction of sin. Cleansing had to wait for the Messiah. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-1-commentary
- Ligonier: John's baptism was preparation, and it is not the same baptism Jesus commanded. Both share the need to repent. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/baptism-john
- **Protestant differences:** Berkhof (Reformed) says John's baptism and Christian baptism are "essentially identical, though differing in some points." He reports that older Lutheran theologians held the two were the same in purpose and effect, though some later Lutherans disagreed. He also doubts that Acts 19 shows anyone being rebaptized. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/berkhof/systematictheology.vii.ii.iv.html
- **Catholic view:**
  - Aquinas: John's baptism did not give grace; it only prepared the way for it. Its "forgiveness of sins" pointed ahead to Christ's baptism. https://www.newadvent.org/summa/4038.htm
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia says It is of Catholic faith that the Precursor's baptism was essentially different in its effects from the baptism of Christ. It adds that what forgave sin was the repentance that went with John's baptism, not the baptism itself. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/02258b.htm
  - Catholic Answers: John could not forgive sins. His baptism was a baptism of repentance that pointed ahead to the sacrament. https://www.catholic.com/qa/how-were-johns-baptisms-different-than-the-sacrament

**v. 5**
- Guzik: John's main message was not "you're a sinner." It was "the Messiah is coming," and repentance was the response to that news. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- Aquinas: those who confessed their sins were not forgiven on the spot through John's baptism. Forgiveness would come through later repentance and Christ's baptism. https://www.newadvent.org/summa/4038.htm

**v. 6**
- Guzik: John was modelled on the bold prophet Elijah (2 Kings 1:8). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/

**v. 7**
- Guzik: John preached Jesus, not himself. Untying sandals was a slave's job that the rabbis said a disciple did not have to do for his teacher, and the Talmud is cited for this. Yet John felt unworthy even to do that. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/

**v. 8**
- Guzik: John's baptism could show repentance. It could not cleanse from sin or give the Spirit the way Jesus would after the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- Gill: John said this to stop people relying on him and his baptism, and to turn them toward Christ. This was spoken to the baptized persons, partly to take off their dependence upon him and his baptism; and partly to direct their views to Christ https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/dby/mark/1-8.html
- Adam Clarke (Methodist): water baptism matters only because it points to, and leads to, the baptism of the Spirit. It is he only who can communicate the Holy Spirit; and water baptism is nothing, but as it points out, and leads to, the baptism of the Holy Ghost. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lsb/mark/1-8.html
- **Protestant differences on when the "baptism with the Spirit" happens:**
  - Sam Storms (charismatic) describes the classical Pentecostal view, which holds that Spirit-baptism is always subsequent to and therefore distinct from conversion. Storms himself disagrees. He holds that all Christians are baptized in the Spirit when they are born again, though he still welcomes later, repeated experiences of the Spirit's power. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/what-is-baptism-in-the-spirit-and-when-does-it-happen--1-corinthians-12:12-13-
  - Bible.org sets out both views. The author argues that Paul in 1 Corinthians 12:13 is describing the same baptism John foretold, which happened at Pentecost. https://bible.org/seriespage/6-holy-spirit-s-ministries-part-iv-baptism-spirit
- **Catholic view:** Aquinas quotes this verse to show that only Christ's baptism cleanses inwardly by the Holy Spirit. https://www.newadvent.org/summa/4038.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik: Jesus was not baptized because He needed cleansing. He did it to do the Father's will and to stand alongside sinful people. Guzik also notes how humble the setting was, citing rabbinic tradition (via Lane) that the Jordan was considered unfit for purification. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- Ligonier: Jesus was baptized to obey the new command God had given His people through John, not because He needed to repent. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/baptism-john
- **Catholic view:** Christ made the waters holy by going down into them, and Christian baptism has its origin in His. His baptism looks ahead to the cross. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/why-jesus-was-baptized
- **A disagreement between traditions:** Joe Heschmeyer (Catholic Answers) agrees with Sinclair Ferguson (Reformed) that Jesus' baptism points to the cross. He rejects Ferguson's view that the cross means God treated the innocent Christ as guilty (penal substitution). He also argues that Christ's baptism makes Christian baptism truly effective, not merely a symbol. https://www.catholic.com/audio/sp/if-jesus-is-sinless-why-was-he-baptized

**v. 10**
- Guzik: the Greek for "breaking open" is strong, suggesting the sky was torn apart. The Spirit was not a dove but came "like" one, and Luke says it took bodily form. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- Precept Austin warns against the early heresy of Cerinthus. He taught that a "Christ spirit" came on the man Jesus at His baptism and left before the cross, which denies both the incarnation and the atonement. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-1-commentary

**v. 11**
- Guzik: Jesus was baptized to be identified *with* sinful people, and the Father's voice identified Him *to* them as His perfect Son. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- Hooker (quoted on Precept Austin): "beloved" was used especially of an only child, which matches John's "only" Son. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-1-commentary
- The Father calls Jesus His Son here and again at the transfiguration (9:7). https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-1-commentary

**vv. 12–13**
- Guzik: Mark suggests the whole forty days were a time of testing, not just the three temptations Matthew and Luke describe. The angels served Him at the end, which shows His authority over both wild animals and angels. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- Precept Austin draws lessons: being tempted is not a sin, testing is God's will, and we are never without God's grace. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/mark-1-commentary
- Precept Austin also says Jesus truly faced temptation but never let it grow into desire. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-1-commentary

**v. 14**
- Guzik: Jesus' ministry centred on preaching. Jesus was a preacher who did wonderful miracles, not a miracle worker who sometimes preached. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/

**v. 15**
- Guzik: to enter the kingdom, people had to change direction. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- A writer quoted on Precept Austin says repentance is what coming to God *is*, not a step before it. Coming to Los Angeles simply means leaving New York. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/mark-1-commentary
- **Views on the kingdom:** Vance Havner (quoted on Precept Austin) says the kingdom came then as God's reign in people's hearts and will come visibly when the King returns. Precept Austin's editor adds that this means a thousand-year reign, which is a premillennial reading. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-1-commentary

**vv. 16–20**
- Peter, Andrew and John had probably met Jesus earlier (John 1:35–42). Here He calls them to leave fishing and follow Him fully and for good. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-1-commentary
- Guzik on v. 17: at root, Christianity is about following Jesus, not theological systems or rules. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/

**vv. 21–22**
- Guzik: the scribes usually quoted a range of rabbis, but Jesus taught boldly, because He had authority and brought a message from God. Guzik adds that authority grows out of submission: Jesus first submitted in His baptism and in the wilderness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/

**Gaps**
- I couldn't read the full Ellicott, Pulpit or Gill comments for most verses, or the NET notes beyond what Precept Austin quotes.
- Nothing from Wesley, Lutheran sites, Assemblies of God (ag.org), or Orthodox sites (oca.org).
- No prosperity or hyper-grace teaching on these verses turned up.
- Almost nothing on vv. 16, 19–21 individually.
